about: An example what-if, not the firm's settings: theirs with every reading measured against the last 30 years instead of the full history.

history.question: Which history is each reading measured against? "full" for everything the publisher has, or {"years": N} for the last N years up to the latest reading.
history.why: Every series starts in a different year, so a fixed window would cut the long ones short; the start of each history is shown beside every reading, as the regulators do.

change_months.question: Over how many months is a change counted? A whole number. Weekly and daily series count whole weeks (12 months is 52), as FRED does: a day with no reading that many weeks before has no change.
change_months.why: A year: it takes out the seasons, and the report reads homeowner's insurance and revolving credit over a year.

normal_width.question: How wide is normal movement? The median change plus or minus this many typical moves, where a typical move is 1.4826 times the median distance of the changes from their median. A number above 0. A change inside reads Stable; one at or past either edge reads Increasing or Decreasing.
normal_width.why: One typical move is the measure the loss thresholds use for ordinary year-to-year movement (threshold-engine scale.py). For changes shaped like a bell it holds about two in three of them, and a spike does not widen it, as it would a standard deviation.

left_out.question: Which quarters are left out of every history? A list, each entry a quarter such as "2020Q2" or a run such as "2020Q2-2021Q2"; [] leaves nothing out. A reading in a quarter left out is not measured against, and a change with either end in one is not counted.
left_out.why: Nothing until there is a reason to record. The pandemic quarters are the usual candidate: 2020Q2 to 2021Q2 holds the spike in jobless claims and unemployment, and the loss thresholds' evidence was tested with and without 2020Q1 to 2023Q4.

axis_cut.question: How much of each chart's readings may run off its axis, at each end? A percent from 0 to 10; 0 keeps every reading on the chart. The latest reading and the normal range always stay on it. Only the charts change; no reading does.
axis_cut.why: A spike such as the 2020 jobless claims flattens the rest of a chart. With 1% at each end it runs off the edge, and a note under the chart names the highest reading and its date.

show_sahm.question: Show the Sahm reading beside the national unemployment rate? true or false.
show_sahm.why: It is the best-known published trigger for unemployment (0.50 points, Sahm 2019), and the report records its false alarm of 2024, so a reader should see it beside the change rather than instead of it.

compare_p.question: On the Dashboard, how small must p be for a link between two series' changes to pass? Two-tailed; a number above 0 and below 1.
compare_p.why: The usual level. A lead is tested at it after allowing for how many leads were tried.

compare_leads.question: On the Dashboard, which leads are tried, in months? A list of whole numbers: a positive lead has the first series moving earlier, a negative one the second.
compare_leads.why: Two years either way and three years of the first leading, in steps of six months: the range the comparison was built with.

compare_starts.question: On the Dashboard, at how many starting points is the one-reading-a-year test run? 1, 2 or 4; the starting months are spread evenly through the year, each the first month of a quarter, so a quarterly series has a reading at every one.
compare_starts.why: Charge-off rates are trailing four-quarter figures, so neighbouring quarters share most of their data; one reading every 12 months keeps them a year apart. Four starting points (a quarter apart) show whether a link holds whichever quarter the count starts from.

compare_min_pairs.question: On the Dashboard, how many one-a-year pairs must a lead have at every starting point to be tested? A whole number of at least 4.
compare_min_pairs.why: Fewer pairs than that cannot show much either way; a lead with fewer says not tested.
